SM Nasirul Haque ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Omar Faruque Chowdhury and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: This Rule was obtained by the preemptor upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and order dated 31-03-99 passed by Additional District Judge, Fifth Court at Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 223 of 1996 affirming those dated 12-10-96 passed by Subordinate Judge, Fourth Court at Dhaka in Preemption Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1992 which disallowed the prayer for preemption.

2. The preemptor made an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, in brief, the Act against the opposite parties for preemption of the transfer of 0.0907 acre of land of SA plot No. 54 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 48/1 out of CS plot No. 139 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 2 by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No.1. His case, in short, is that said khatian No. 2 consisted of 5 plots of which CS plot No.139 comprised of 3.49 acre of land. Owners of other plots got settlements from the Bhowal Raj Court of Wards Estate by opening separate holdings. The CS plot No. 139 was joint and still remained joint and other owners of other four plots were never co-sharers in this plot.

3. Lal Mahmud, Waz Mahmud, Shukur Mahmud and Noor Mahmud took settlement of 2.36 acres from said Court of Wards Estate and the rest 1.13 acre was given settlement to Ibrahim and his brother Wasimuddin. Said Lal Mahmud and three others transferred their land to Nishi Kanta Shome, Rebati Mohan Shome and Amrita Lal Shome. Then, one Golam Mowla purchased the said land from them by deed No. 5935 dated 27-08-51 and deed No. 6755 dated 27-09-51 and became owner in possession. Similarly, Ibrahim and his brother transferred their land to one Charu Bala. Thereafter, the land was sold in auction for arrears of rents and one Jamsher Ali purchased said land measuring 1.13 acre in the auction. The auction was confirmed on 23-12-49 and possession was delivered to him on 31-01-50.

4. While Jamsher Ali was thus owner in possession in 1.13 acre, he transferred 0.4050 acre by a registered deed dated 03-05-50 to one Mainuddin and the rest 0.7250 acre by another registered deed dated 22-01-51 to Hasina Shamsuddin, opposite party No. 7 Mainuddin on the same date re-transferred his land to Hasina Shamsuddin. Thus, Hasina Shamsuddin became owner in possession of said 1.13 acre of land.

5. Golam Mowla also on 27-08-51 transferred 0.70 acre to one Haji Tarikullah by a registered deed and to one Noor Akhter Khatun 0.5250 acre by another deed. He then on 30-04-53 transferred 11 decimals to late SM Nazmul Huque, father of the preemptor and 22 decimals to opposite party No. 29, mother of the preemptor, and on 20-07-54 further transferred 30 decimals to the father of the preemptor. Similarly, Golam Mowla transferred the rest of his land at different times to different persons, and thus, he exhausted all his interest in said 2.36 acre of land of CS plot No. 139. The parents of the preemptor thus became owners in possession in total 0.63 acre of land out of CP plot No.139.

6. Haji Tarikullah instituted Partition Suit No. 43 of 1993 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka for partition. Father of the preemptor is defendant No.3 in the suit. The parents of the preemptor jointly prayed for a 'Saham' in respect of their purchased land of 0.63 acre. The suit was on 15-12-54 decreed in the preliminary form the suit was then transferred to the Fourth Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka and was re-numbered as Partition Suit No. 584 of 1993. The suit is still pending for final decree. Further case of the preemptor is that CS plot No. 139 was never partitioned by metes and bound and, as such, he is still a co-sharer in said land and is therefore entitled to pre-empt. Having come to know about the transfer of the case land by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No. 1, the application was filed on making the statutory deposit.

7. Opposite party, No. 1 opposed the prayer for preemption by filing a written objection. Main objection is that during the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 number of plots was created out of said CS Khatian No. 139 under various khatians on the basis of possession of the persons. As the land measuring 0.63 acre was recorded in a new SA plot No.92 appertaining to first SA Khatian No.76 then 73 in the names of the parents of the preemptor, so, the land of opposite party No. 2 including the transferred land was recorded in separate SA plot No. 54 appertaining to SA khatian No. 48/1. The opposite party No. 2, vendor and others exclusively possessed their respective lands on payment of rents since the record of rights was finally published in 1964. Similarly, all other owners of the rest land of original CS plot No. 139 now exclusively possess their respective land either on the basis of SA record of rights or by subsequent mutations. The preemptor was not a co-sharer in the holding of opposite party No. 2 and, as such, his application was liable to be dismissed.

8. Opposite party Nos. 21 and 22 also filed an objection and adopted the case as made out by the preemptor as they appear to be the sisters of the preemptor.

9. On the aforesaid pleadings, five issues were raised of which the moot issue was whether the preemptor is a co-sharer in the disputed jote.

10. One witness each was examined on behalf of the preemptor and opposite party No. 1. Number of documents was produced by both the parties, which were marked as exhibits.

11. The learned Subordinate Judge found the preemptor not a co-sharer in the land and accordingly, disallowed the application. On appeal therefrom at the instance .of the preemptor, the learned Additional District Judge hearing the same was also pleased to affirm the decision of the trial Court, and dismissed the appeal by impugned judgment and order.

12. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner read section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 and submits that the preemptor is still a co-sharer in the land of CS plot No. 139 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 2 and the Courts below erred in law in disallowing preemption on the view that the preemptor is not a co-sharer in land. Elaborating, he submits that CS plot 139 was never partitioned by metes and bound and until a final decree in the Partition Suit is passed the preemptor must be held to be a co-sharer in said land. In support, he cites the decisions in the case of Muhammad Muzaffar Khan vs Muhammad Yusuf Khan, 11 DLR (SC) 78, SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 230 and Shafiuddin Chowdhury vs Md Abdul Karim and others, 52 DLR (AD) 41.

13. Opposing the Rule, Mr. Md Ismail, learned Counsel for the purchaser, opposite party No. 1 submits that the land measuring 3.49 as was recorded as CS plot in 1917-18 in the Cadastral survey was split up in numerous plots under various khatians during the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in 1964 and the persons including the preemptor have been exclusively possessing their respective land according to such record of rights. The parents of the preemptor were in exclusive possession in their 0.63 acre of land which was recorded as SA plot No. 92 under SA khatian No. 73 Exhibit 'Ka' while opposite party No. 2 was in exclusive possession in plot No. 54 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 4811. The preemptor is therefore not a co-sharer in the land transferred by the kabala Exhibit No. 8. He accordingly, submits that the learned Additional District Judge did not commit any error in affirming the order of the trial Court in disallowing preemption. He also submits that everyone of purchasers of land of said CS plot No. 139 including the parents of the preemptor got their names mutated and in view of provisions of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the parents of the preemptor ceased to be co-sharer in said land. In support, he cites the decisions in the case of Haladar Dutta vs Abdul Rob Chowdhury, 36 DLR 193 and Md Khairullah vs Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 338.

14. Only question facing us is whether the learned Additional District Judge is well founded in affirming the decision of the trial Court in disallowing the application for preemption. More precisely, the issue raised for our decision is whether the preemptor is a co-sharer in the land transferred by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No. 1 by a sale deed No. 1677 dated 30-06-91, Exhibit No.8 within the meaning of section 24 of the Act, 1949.

15. We have perused the record, and heard the learned counsels at length. We shall first consider the cases as cited by them.

<u>16. Muhammad Muzaffar Khan vs Muhammad Yusuf Khan, 11 DLR (SC) 76 arose out of two suits for preemption. Khatian No. 324 of a village in the District of DI Khan, comprising of 54 Khasras and measuring 2664 kanals 1 maria in area were jointly owned and possessed by two brothers, Samundar and Qalandar in equal shares, and the rest half belonged to Alamgir Khan. Muhammad Muzaffar Khan, the appellant, purchased 480 kanals of different khasras of the khata from said Alamgir Khan. No partition was ever effected. Co-sharers possessed in severalty specific shares. Samundar and Qalandr jointly sold 62 kanals to respondent Muhammad Yusuf Khan. A mutation followed. Subsequently, Samundar sold another 30 kanals to said Yusuf Khan. The appellant instituted the suits for preemption of these two sales as co-sharer.</u>

<u>"A plain consideration of nature of the transaction in the circumstances of this case could, in our opinion, lead to but one conclusion. The vendee of a co-sharer who owns an undivided khata in common with another is clothed with the same rights as the vendor has in the property, no more and no less. If the vendor was in exclusive possession of a certain portion of the joint land and transfers its possession to his vendee, so long as there is no partition between the co-sharers, the vendee must be regarded as stepping into the shoes of his transferor qua his ownership rights in the joint property, to the extent of the area purchased by him, provided that the area in question does not exceed the share which the transferor owns in the whole property. Alienation of specific plots transferred to the vendee would only entitle the latter to retain possession of them till such time as an actual partition by metes and bounds takes place between the co-sharers. It is difficult to see in these circumstances why the vendee of specific plots acquired from a co-owner, in an undivided khata, does not become a co-sharer in the khata. It may be pointed out that the mutations in favour of the appellant, which are on the record, described the sale transactions in his favour as hissadari sales of the joint khata in suit.</u>

<u>Upon such finding, the Supreme Court of Pakistan restored the decision of first two Courts allowing preemption. What Khata, khasras, kanals etc, means, we could not ascertain. Nor we could ascertain the land law in Peshawar at the time. Unlike our land tenure, the land laws there, particularly, in the then West Pakistan was tilted a bit to big land holdings, Besides, unless the law for preemption in Peshawar is not in pari-materia with our law, i.e. the Act, 1949, in brief, the Act, 1949, it is very difficult for us to follow the opinion of the Pakistan Supreme Court. Moreover, if we take Khata meaning a tenancy or holding, the above view of the Supreme Court of Pakistan will be of no help because sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act have provided procedure for amalgamation and subdivision of a tenancy or holding, and after a valid subdivision of a holding and distribution of the rents, preemption at the instance of a co-sharer of the former joint holding is not maintainable.</u>

17. SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 230 arose out of an application under section 24 of the Act, 1949. The case land appertained to a permanent tenure recorded in CS Khatian No. 214 in the names of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani. Akshoy instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 for partition and by the decree passed, Akshoy got one-third share while Rangubala got the rest two-third. One Nafisa Khatun purchased the entire share of Akshoy by a registered sale deed dated 19-07-52 while Rangubala settled her share of two-third for 99 years by a registered deed of lease dated 23-12-53 with Ayesha Khatun, respondent No. 2. Then, Nafisa Khatun sold her share to respondent No. 1 by a registered deed of sale dated 18-04-72. Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant by a registered deed of sale dated 10- 09-73. Against this sale, respondent No.1 filed the application for preemption, which was allowed by the trial Court. Against the order, appellant's appeal and revision failed. But the Appellate Division set aside the order and dismissed the application for preemption. But, we find, on different reasons.

18. The main issue as to whether respondent No.1 was a co-sharer in land along with other questions were considered and determined in the appeal. Mr Ruhul Islam, J, wrote the leading judgment. Construing the phrase, 'Non-Agricultural land' His Lordship was of the view,

"Different sub-sections of section 24 sufficiently indicate that the Legislature did not use the expression 'Non-Agricultural land' carrying the same meaning as the expression 'holding' defined in the Bengal Tenancy Act and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The expression 'Non-Agricultural land' may represent the entire land comprised in a tenancy or it may form a part as owned and possessed by a tenant or tenants on partition."

While concurring with the conclusion allowing the appeal, Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed, J, as his Lordship then was, on the point reserved his verdict as hereunder,

"Secondly, a Full Bench of the High Court in the case of 'Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury vs Rezia Begum'; 16 DLR 77 examined this question and by majority decision held that these two terms, 'Non-Agricultural land' and 'holding', are synonymous carrying the same meaning, Since this question is not necessary for disposal of the instant appeal, I would refrain from expressing any opinion as to the correctness of the decision of the High Court in that case."

19. Before this decision, it appears, the view of the Full Bench in the case of Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury was holding the field that the phrase and word 'Non-Agricultural land' and 'holding', are synonymous carrying the same meaning.

20. In holding that the respondent No. 1 was a co-sharer in the land, their Lordships gave different reasons as well. Mr Ruhul Islam, J was of the view,

"In this case also by effecting partition on the basis of a decree of the Civil Court the co- sharers, namely, Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Chouwdhurani possessed separately the land in their respective share, but the tenancy with the jama of Rs 10 was not divided or split up."

Lastly, he found,

"In view of what has been stated above, in my opinion the respondents not being co-sharer in the land transferred, though they may be co- sharer in the tenancy, the right of preemption did not accrue in their favour and, as such, their application for preemption must fail."

Whereas, Mr Shahabuddin Ahmend, J finds,

"The principle of law on this subject is that where an under-raiyati is created by a raiyat, the latter is not a co-sharer of the former; and when the superior interest of the raiyat is extinguished and he disappears, the under-raiyat is upgraded into a raiyat but only in respect of his own share. If the previous raiyat or for that matter his co-sharer raiyat held khas any portion of the original tenancy, that portion becomes a separate raiyati under the Government with which the upgraded raiyat has got no connection. In view of the position, the under-raiyati held by Ayesha upgraded into an independent raiyati which got no connection with the raiyati previously held by Nafisa, now by respondent No.1 As such, respondent No.1 is not a co-sharer of the appellant and he got no right to pre-empt the land purchased by the appellant from Ayesha Khatun."

Mr Ruhul Islam, J found that respondent No.1 was not a co-sharer on the basis of the decree passed in the suit for partition, under which the land was separated though the tenancy remained the same while Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed J was of the view, that after the wholesale acquisition, the under-raiyati of Ayesha Khatun was upgraded into an independent raiyati which got no connection with the raiyati held by Nafisa, now by respondent No.I. Mr Ruhul Islam, J is therefore of the view that the decree in partition suit results in separation and division of the land. But Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed expressed himself as follows.

" .....by a decree in a partition suit the parties go into separate and exclusive possession of their respective shares in the land of a holding, but such a decree does not result in the splitting up of the holding along with its jama which may be done only by sub-division of the holding under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, corresponding to section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Right of preemption is not extinguished by partition as was rightly held in the case of Md Shukur vs Ram Chandra Kapali, 6 DLR 393. This principle however will apply only in the case of a 'holding'. Whether this principle will be applicable in the case of a non-agricultural tenancy will depend upon the question whether 'Non-Agricultural Land' under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the 'holding' under section 26 F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, corresponding to section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are synonymous carrying the same meaning."

As quoted above that he refrained from expressing any opinion on the question.

21. Before the above case, on May 5, 1982 the Appellate Division in the case of Md Khairullah vs Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury as cited above by a majority of 3:2 disallowed the prayer for preemption under section 24 of the Act, 1949 on the ground of amalgamation and separation of old holding. In the leading judgment written by Mr Ruhul Islam J, the preemptor was found to be not a co-sharer on the view.

"Amalgamation of tenancies made in Miscellaneous Case No. 89/72-73 under sections 116 and 117(1)(a) was given effect by amending khatian No. 14 after excluding plot No. 108 therefrom and revenue was collected on the basis of the new khatian No. 18. Prima facie the order was a valid one; its validity could not be challenged for a collateral purpose, that is, in a proceeding of preemption. The Civil Court while dealing with altogether a different matter cannot ignore the order passed by a competent Revenue Officer under section 117 of the Act."

22. In the Case of Shafiuddin Chowdhury vs Md Abdul Karim, in allowing a review of its earlier decision, the Appellate Division disallowed the prayer for preemption on the ground of partition of the land by a decree. It held that,

"the passing of the final decree in a partition suit finally determines the rights of the co-sharers in land. Hence, the application for the preemptor-respondents on the basis of co- sharer ship is not maintainable."

23. Ratio decidendi in the above decisions is that a decree of the Court in a partition suit brings separation and division in the joint possession and enjoyment of land. But such decree does not ipso facto result in the splitting of holding along with the jama till such subdivision of the holding and distribution of the rents takes place in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act or the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the case may be. Such division of the land may also be brought about by an amicable partition among the co-sharers in such land. But the main submission of Mr. Islam is that the total area of land in a plot as was plotted in the cadastral survey in 1917-18 must to be taken as an undivided unit. If such land was recorded in the names of more than one person, all such persons and/or their successors-in-interest must be held to be co-sharers in such plot till the land is partitioned by a decree of the Court or by amicable partition among such co-sharers. Even any sub-division of such CS plot and/or the holding to which such plot appertained in subsequent survey, say, under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 will not result in the termination of co-sharer ship in such land and thereby, taking away the right of preemption under section 24 of the Act, 1949. The argument appears to be unique in the sense that it was never argued since the Act came into force in 1949. We are unable to accept such interpretation of the law.

<u>24. Firstly, we do not find any reason or authority to agree with Mr Islam that the word 'land' as used in the expression 'co-sharer in the land' in section 24(1) of the Act, 1949 should always mean the quantum of land in one plot only. As the word 'co-sharer' always implies the existence of more than one person jointly owning, similarly, such joint ownership may be in respect of land of one plot or several plots. It is now well settled rule of interpretation as to number that in every Act, unless the contrary intention appears, the words in the singular shall include the plural, the words in the plural shall include singular. The land is always recorded under a holding for the purpose of revenue record and payment of rents. This holding may be joint of several persons, or exclusive in the name of one person. It may also may be noted that the holding of any land, agricultural or non-agricultural, could only be sub-divided and rents distributed in accordance with the procedure under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. But the proposition of Mr Islam that such sub-division of the holding and distribution of rents will not affect the land appertaining to such holding is equally misconceived.</u>

<u>25. Secondly, who are the co-sharers in the expression, 'co-sharer in the land'? To find the answer, we need not go far just to refer to the holding, more popularly known as khatian, comprising of such land. The concept of 'co-sharer' cannot be conceived independent of any holding or tenancy. If the holding is recorded in the name of more than one person, then, each of such person or his successor-in-interest is the co-sharer to each other in such land. Such a co-sharer will deem to continue as such co-owner in both holding as well as in land so long the holding will continue to be joint. Contrary to such proposition as argued by Mr Islam that sub-division of such holding will not affect the land in any way appear to be fallacious. Because, after sub-division of the holding and creation of new plots in subsequent survey, or by mutation by the acts of parties, the previous co- owners in the holding and/or the land cannot be deemed to still continue as such co-owners.</u>

<u>26. Coming to the facts of this case, we find, on 30-04-53 and 30-07-54 parents of the preemptor purchased 0.63 acre of land. After the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 their purchased land was recorded as plot No. 92 appertaining to first khatian No. 76 and then, No. 73, Exhibit 'Ka', Accordingly, they possessed since then, and after them, the preemptor has been in possession and enjoying the land on payment of rents in the separate jama. His possession and enjoyment are absolutely independent and exclusive of others. Similarly, the land transferred by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No. 1 vide sale deed No. 1677 dated 30-06-91 was recorded as SA plot No. 54 appertaining SA khatian No.48/1. In the partition suit, the father of the preemptor as defendant No. 3 along with defendant No. 2 and defendant Nos. 4 to 6 prayed for saham and the preliminary decree dated 15-12-54 has allotted a saham to each of those defendants on the basis of their purchase. Mr Islam told that effecting partition by Advocate Commissioners failed four times. Mr Ismail submitted that chance of any final decree is far remote for the present successors of the original plaintiff have lost all their interest in such a decree. Be that as it may, the final decree that may ultimately be passed will just formalise independent and exclusive possession of present owners. The submission of Mr Islam that even after so many transactions and transfers since the final publication of CS record of rights, and the long and exclusive possession and enjoyment by the present occupiers on the basis of SA record of rights and/or mutation have not yet terminated the original co- sharer ship in CS plot No.139 as recorded in 1917-18 cannot be accepted.</u>

<u>27. In view of above decisions, there is no escape from the irresistible conclusion that even if the land in the expression, 'co-sharer in the land' in section 24(1) of the Act, 1949 is not synonymous to a holding but conceiving of such land without reference to the word 'co-sharer' is neither feasible nor possible. And the word 'co-sharer' in the phrase 'co-sharer in the land' is the key to find whether the preemptor is entitled to pre-empt. A final decree passed in a partition suit or amicable partition though separates and divides the land for the purpose of possession but does not ipso Jacto terminate co-ownership in such land till subdivision of the holding and distribution of rents takes place only in accordance with law. Sub-division of a holding and distribution of rents may also take place in a revenue survey subsequent to the cadastral survey with or without the plot or plots divided into different small plots. As stated above, such sub-division may also take place at the instance of one or more of the co-tenants of the holding in accordance with the provisions of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Such sub-division always terminates the joint tenancy or more precisely co-sharership in the land, no matter whether the land is sub-divided or separated or not and after such sub-division, the old co-owners of the holding in such land cannot be deemed to still continue as co-sharer in the land within the meaning of section 24(1) of the Act, 1949.</u>

28. Lastly, it is now well settled by the decision of our Appellate Division that all lands situate within a municipal area must be deemed to be non-agricultural land for the purpose of preemption. We cannot think of the disastrous consequence of the view as Mr Islam submits that the quantum of land as recorded in one plot in the name of more than one person during the cadastral survey in 1917-18 must be deemed to be an independent unit and in the joint ownership of those persons as recorded then till partition by metes and bound-to declare all such land still joint for the purpose of preemption. Such view will definitely go against the public policy as well.

29. In the facts and circumstances of the case, and on the above principles, we could not find any reason to differ from the concurrent conclusion of the Courts below that the preemptor ceased to be a co-sharer in the land in question and, as such, his application for preemption was rightly found to be not maintainable. No failure of justice has occasioned by the decision.

30. In the result, the Rule is discharged with costs. Impugned judgment and order affirming the order of the trial Court in disallowing the application for preemption are confirmed. Order of stay as granted at the time of issue of the Rule is hereby recalled and vacated.

Send down the records.

End.
